newsitem.title: USA: OUTLOOK--Waning distillate fears seen cooling heat.
newsitem.headline: OUTLOOK--Waning distillate fears seen cooling heat.

text.p: Upward pressure on heating oil prices should relent given views that low distillate stocks may begin building more quickly amid record output by refiners, traders and analysts said.

"We have never seen this rate of distillate production before. If it continues we could see higher distillate builds and that might take some steam out of the high prices," said Prudential Securities energy analyst Robert Baker.
American Petroleum Institute (API) said U.S. refiners cranked out 3.6 million barrels per day (bpd) of distillates for the week ending October 11.
The federal Energy Information Administration showed refineries running at 94.9 percent of their capacity for the four weeks ending October 11, versus 93.8 percent during the same period last year.

Despite the voluminous output, traders said stock builds have lagged because as many as four million barrels of heating oil and low sulfur diesel have been exported to Europe in the past month as that region ushers in low sulphur diesel fuel.

"But the arbitrage window is fairly well closed now, except for some Euro spec low sulfur diesel," one East Coast trader said Monday, adding that a combination of waning exports and heavy domestic production is likely to boost inventories.
An unexpected cold snap or reopening of the arb window, however, could wreak havoc on that hopeful scenario, traders cautioned.
Players said they expected gasoline in New York Harbor and the Gulf Coast to follow the lead of heating oil and crude oil.
And in the Midwest, traders expected gasoline prices to continue easing while low sulphur diesel prices were seen surging higher on spot buying, particularly in the Group.
"I think there should be some additional softening on gasoline in the Group," said Laura Anello, broker with FCC-Penterra in Kansas City, Mo. "There's plenty of gas around."

Some traders said agricultural demand appeared to peak last week, while others said there were several weeks remaining in the autumn harvest and tightness in diesel barrels could fuel rising differentials by late October.
The Williams pipeline system, a key barometer of inventories in the Group, reported a 21-day supply of gasoline with a large shipment expected at month-end and a 23-day supply of low sulphur diesel.
West Coast traders forecast stable prices, as high crude prices continue to wreck havoc on refinery profits.
"I'll think you'll see a sideways market," a West Coast broker said.

A 21 percent slide in fourth quarter margins could force West Coast refiners to cut runs in coming weeks, traders said. They added that Tosco and Ultramar were rumored to be considering cutbacks, with Ultramar declining to buy crude for November.
-- Ransdell Pierson, New York Energy Desk 212 859-1632
